source.title: Impact of L1 Batch Normalization on Analog Noise Resistant Property of Deep Learning Models

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 models with different BatchNorm types and measures how weight noise affects inference accuracy. This extends the claim's CIFAR training setting to noise resistance, but it does not measure training classification error.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's training and clean baseline accuracy results, which are explicit outcomes relevant to V6's claim that normalization choices affect training performance. The weight-noise robustness results do not measure the claim's training-error outcome, so they are not rows for the listed versions. Figures 1 and 2 give condition-specific noise results only as plots; the text also provides selected numeric examples and aggregate values in Table III.
record.test_reason: The study relies on BatchNorm's training benefits when designing its models, but tests clean test accuracy and robustness to weight noise during inference. It reports no training-speed comparison, learning-rate-tolerance comparison, or BatchNorm-free control. Its own results therefore test none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that L1 and TopK BatchNorm improve resistance to additive Gaussian weight noise while retaining competitive clean inference accuracy. They also conclude that robustness depends on classification-task complexity. Their conclusion concerns inference robustness and accuracy, not demonstrated training acceleration.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares normalization types and evaluates additive Gaussian weight-noise robustness, rather than testing the original batch-normalization training-speed claim. Training uses PyTorch defaults, categorical cross-entropy, SGD, data augmentation, and runs until convergence.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported clean baseline inference accuracy varies by dataset, architecture, and BatchNorm type. For the noise-resistance outcome, the authors report differences by BatchNorm type, architecture, dataset, and noise factor; the tested noise factors are 1%, 4%, 8%, 12%, 16%, and 20%.

fits_no_version.finding: Table II compares clean test accuracy after convergence among L2, L1, and TopK BatchNorm variants; all models use BatchNorm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: L1 and TopK BatchNorm variants can retain competitive clean inference accuracy relative to L2 BatchNorm on the tested CIFAR architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 1–2 and Table III report greater normalized inference accuracy under additive Gaussian weight noise for L1 and TopK variants than L2 variants. For DenseNet100 on CIFAR-10 at 20% noise, the reported values are 90.90%, 89.18%, and 11.64%, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changing BatchNorm from L2 to L1 or TopK can improve inference robustness to additive Gaussian weight noise in the tested models.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Network
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. Noise robustness is evaluated with additive Gaussian weight noise and test inference accuracy; the text does not describe a capability check relevant to the catalog's training-error claim. Many noise-factor outcomes are shown only in figures, and the text gives selected examples and averages rather than exact per-condition values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from Table II baseline inference accuracy results. Figure 1, Figure 2, and Table III noise-robustness outcomes are outside the listed versions because they measure inference degradation under injected weight noise, not training error, training speed, or learning-rate tolerance.

untested.parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and additional student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth, plain versus residual networks, and special initialization or normalization-free training.
Initialization comparisons, signal and gradient propagation, training speed, and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, transient loss growth, curvature changes, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence.

All parts: acceleration and higher-learning-rate tolerance from adding BatchNorm, and Fixup training without normalization. Comparing final test accuracy among BatchNorm variants does not test these outcomes.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded values are post-training test-set inference accuracies at zero injected noise; their operation should be inference evaluation. Training until convergence does not establish near-zero training classification error. The paper's statements about BatchNorm accelerating or stabilizing training rely on prior work. Noise-robustness results are already declared in rows_left_out and supply no missing evidence for V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: Training error, corrupted or random labels, model size effects, early stopping, and regularized recipes are not measured.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and student width are not tested.
Plain versus residual shortcut training error across depth is not compared.
Initialization effects on signal propagation, training speed, or trainable depth are not tested.
Learning rates relative to stability limits, loss trajectories, and sharpness are not tested.

The paper compares L2, L1, and TopK BatchNorm variants on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 baseline inference accuracy, but does not report accuracy-versus-training-time, higher-learning-rate tolerance, sigmoid networks on MNIST, VGG on CIFAR-10, Inception on ImageNet, or Fixup without normalization.
